newsitem.title: USA: Costs, benefits of cholestrol-cutting drug studied.
newsitem.headline: Costs, benefits of cholestrol-cutting drug studied.

text.p: It pays to give heart patients medicine to reduce their cholesterol levels, according to a cost-benefit analysis in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

After showing three years ago that treating people with the drug simvastatin lowers cholesterol levels and reduces overall mortality, members of the Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study Group looked at how much it costs to extend a person's life by an extra year.

Treatment with simvastatin, sold under the brand name Zocor by Merck, cost about $604 per year in Sweden. The researchers estimated the price of medical care that would be unnecessary if patients cut their cholesterol levels by using the drug.

"The cost of each year of life gained ranged from $3,800 for 70-year-old men with 309 milligrams of cholesterol per deciliter to $27,400 for 35-year-old women with 213 milligrams of cholesterol per deciliter," concluded the group, led by Dr. Magnus Johannesson of the Stockholm School of Economics.

The study group concluded that the price tag was worth it. When they included indirect costs such as the amount of income a person would lose each year through illness or death, the benefits clearly outweighed the cost, the researchers said.
Among both men and women age 35 with heart disease, no matter what their cholesterol counts, giving simvastatin produced a net savings.

The researchers stressed that their findings apply only to people who have heart disease. The results do not mean that health care costs could be reduced by giving the drug to everyone because "the absolute risks of coronary heart disease are substantially lower" in the general population.
